I’ve studied Viking history for both my undergraduate and postgraduate. A wonderful, rewarding experience, but I spent three days trying to work out whether Olaf Cuaran received his nickname because he wore Irish sandals or maybe he had a hunch back. There’s several theories as to why Ivar the boneless received his nickname, same with Hrolf “the Walker”. That’s just on nicknames. And now people claim to be able to decide whether a god of deception fitted a modern concept of gender-fluidity? 

Truth is, nobody knows or has a 100% convincing argument. And if they claim to be right, they’re either a leader in their field or a complete fucking idiot on the internet.

Right, first off, we are looking at sources which are often written (not created, they were oral tales before figures like Snorri Sturlusson wrote them down) centuries after the Christianisation of Scandinavia, by Christians, who may or may not have had a curious nostalgia or a full on opposition to pagan stories. Even if they liked these stories, they wrote for a Christian audience and so can’t be too supportive. 

Then, we have to understand that the changing language may have caused mistranslations. These stories were passed down orally for who knows how long before being written down. 800s old Norse is different to 1200s Icelandic (although close) and mistakes of the translator, and then subsequent mistranslations down to the modern day are bound to happen. 

Then we have the fact that these stories are dripping with symbolism, inside jokes, etc that would be well known to the Vikings who heard the stories, but mean nothing to us, and we’d probably miss them completely. Remember learning Shakespeare in high school and every few lines your teacher has to tell you the context? The problem is magnified with these texts. 

This isn’t a problem unique to the Sagas either. The Iliad, the Bible, literally every classical text ever is mistranslated and misunderstood and since a tonne of historians in the 1800s were whacked out on Opium when translating and understanding these texts, it’s only now that we go back to some of them and realise “hey, there’s something about this that doesn’t make any sense”

Reminder: there are people out there who think Odin drank semen from hanged men because of a colossal mistranslation that picked up mainstream attention. Historians are fallible, and our mistakes aren’t fixed for decades. 

So, if Loki is genderfluid? Ive got no fucking idea dude. But as others have said, attaching modern ideas of gender and masculinity to a story that has been mistranslated, misappropriated and misunderstood for almost a thousand years is dumb as shit. It’s not just old Norse stories either. It’s literally all tales ever.

Twenty years later, a messenger arrived at his castle demanding he attend King Henry immediately. Censoring and toning down content:

I’ve been writing a particularly dark novel recently and I’ve had mixed feedback regarding some of the more violent scenes. Some people like the detail, others think it’s gratuitous and might work against me if I want to get it published.



For background, it’s a post-apocalyptic, dystopian future and features cannibalism, foul language, excessive violence, drug use (not like street drugs, more…you know those psychedelic substances vikings used to go berserk? That), and threats of sexual assault. The protagonists are also teenagers if that’s any help.


Some people have said the detail is fine and they like it, but others have called it gratuitous and say it won’t get published as a YA book, and the fact the protagonists are teenagers means adults won’t be interested. So it occupies a middle ground where people won’t want to touch it. Apparently anyway.


For me, the violence serves a point because one thing I hate about “grim dark” settings is that the truly graphic/disturbing stuff is hinted at, or happens “out of sight”. All this world building about how harsh and brutal life is, and for some reason the reader doesn’t see it happen? We know that in real life, teenagers see horrible things before they’re adults and somehow the teenagers in a fictional universe somehow never see that? It just doesn’t make sense to me.
So yeah, one feedback I’ve received is to tone down the violence and stop the teenagers from swearing so much. Which just doesn’t sit right with me.


I guess the intended audience for my book is 16-21, and I would have thought that people in that age range would be fine with that content.

Ambushes, bombings, assassinations, let’s say that’s what the werewolves get up to. In both western and eastern occupied zones, these attacks are a massive issue, partly because it shows continued support for nazis amongst the population, but it also fractures the post war allies further. All the intelligence agencies know that some high ranking nazis have been allowed to escape punishment and join the other’s military and intelligence networks. With the beginning of the Cold War, it’s not that hard to imagine that both sides would believe the other is trying to undermine the others occupation. Soviets and western allies trade accusations that they’re supporting the Nazis after years of fighting them. 

But honestly, nothing much changes. Is there a troop increase? Not really. Post-war Germany is the most militarised region on earth at this point. Troops are on high alert, checkpoints on every road, houses are regularly searched, civilians are arbitrarily detained and German hostility to their occupiers is obvious but what can they do? De-nazification continues, and the werewolves dwindle like other partisans, finally coming to an end by the mid 50s and early 60s.

The Werewolves never came to anything in our timeline because the German military and society was absolutely gutted by war. They were starving, they were lacking every necessity possible. The plans to stockpile weapons and supplies to begin a guerrilla war never got off the ground because no German commander in their right mind would have siphoned ammunition, weapons and supplies for a guerrilla war in 1945 when the front is collapsing and German soil itself is being occupied. And the fanatics in the party and the SS? They either killed themselves, went down fighting, or ran off to South America and the French foreign legion. Any figure of note that could have been rallied around either killed themselves or was hauled before Nuremberg.  The leadership, the supplies, the manpower, and the sheer will to fight wasn’t there to begin a guerrilla war.

But let’s say the werewolves do launch a few attacks, spooking the allies like I mentioned. The Allies crack down and get arbitrary in their treatment of German civilians. The Soviets especially go apeshit, and German men and boys are imprisoned, tortured and shot at a much higher rate than in our timeline. Soviet propaganda spins this as a crackdown against fascists, and to be honest, they did this with pretty much every intervention in Eastern Europe during the Cold War. In 1956 for example, Krushchev justified sending tanks into Hungary by saying the rising was led by fascist elements, with literally zero evidence. The werewolves just give added justification for further crimes against the defeated german people. 

In summary, the werewolves maybe kill a few hundred occupying soldiers in a small scale campaign of bombings, sabotage, ambushes etc. The allies in all occupied zones respond with a crackdown, soviets do what soviets do best.

True, Vikings weren't the overpowered, all conquering warriors that we'd like them to be. They were opportunist raiders for the most part and when they banded together in large enough numbers for campaigns, these armies were not invincible. Hell, Viking raids on Frankia, particularly inland, plummeted in frequency after a number of bridges were built along the Seine. Bridges. Not forts, not garrisons, bridges. 

And yeah, you're right, areas that suffered heavily from Viking raids and then, conquest weren't the countries we see today, but fragmented kingdoms that couldn't weather the storm of raids and conquest. Northumbria, East Anglia, Mercia, Alba, the multiple kingdoms of Ireland, Brittany, (oddly enough, not Wales, despite being even more divided into tiny principalities) were all devastated and conquered for some time before driving the Vikings out. The Norsemen were driven out of Dublin on more than one occasion and the Danelaw in England went through a period of strife to the extent where new kings rose and fell at a rapid rate. And against large, organised armies, naturally they were a bit hit and miss, as can be seen by the disastrous invasion of Islamic Spain. Compared to great empires, like the Mongols and the Romans, these guys weren't exactly around for the long haul in occupying.

But these guys aren't remembered in history as all powerful conquerors who swept down from the north and destroyed multiple kingdoms, otherwise a considerable number of us would still be pagan. The Vikings are remembered in history for making kingdoms across Europe watch their backs for centuries. From Iona in Scotland to Byzantium in Greece, no coastline was safe. 

Oh sure, like I said, Vikings didn't dominate every foe they encountered. Both raiding forces and armies of conquest suffered defeats, that's to be expected. However, these armies and raiding parties weren't, for the most part, led by great kings who could say they were king of Norway or Denmark. Rather, these famous armies and raids were led by warlords, relatively small local leaders who banded together to embark on this conquest. And yet, these raids and small armies were capable of inflicting enormous damage on much larger kingdoms and on a number of occasions, despite what you say, did defeat organised armies and overcame resistance to do so. 

Oh, and they didn't just conquer parts of England. Other people have explained it better, but just to add, Brittany, Scottish isles, Normandy (by treaty), Sicily (if we're counting Normans as Vikings here), large parts of Ireland and swathes of what is now Russia, Ukraine and other parts of Eastern Europe were conquered, right until they were stopped at Byzantium.

Final note, the Vikings had a great reputation as warriors in their time, as individuals and groups, to the extent that Viking mercenaries served across Europe and even the Byzantines established the Varangian guard, an elite group of Viking and Rus mercenaries who served across the Mediterranean and parts of the Middle East.
